name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
title: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
answer: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL. The major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This scope covers batch and interactive SQL workloads, feature stores, and in-database inference for scoring, classification, and generation. It also includes the metadata and governance layers that make warehouse tables usable as training and serving inputs.

sections.body: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL. The major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This scope covers batch and interactive SQL workloads, feature stores, and in-database inference for scoring, classification, and generation. It also includes the metadata and governance layers that make warehouse tables usable as training and serving inputs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A warehouse or lakehouse for AI typically runs on a cloud object store for raw files, a SQL engine over columnar formats such as Parquet, and a catalog that tracks tables and schemas. Compute is separated from storage, so query clusters and model serving endpoints can scale independently. Some platforms add vector indexes and model registries alongside the SQL engine. The site tracks 262 active Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, which shows how external AI systems connect to these platforms through a common interface.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts and engineers prepare data with SQL transformations, often landing raw events in a lakehouse and building curated tables with transformation tools. For AI work, features are computed in SQL and stored in feature tables, then models are trained outside the warehouse or with in-database machine learning functions. Inference can run as SQL user-defined functions or as model serving endpoints that read directly from governed tables. The Model Context Protocol servers tracked by this site let an AI assistant issue SQL queries and retrieve results without moving the underlying data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance for warehouse and lakehouse AI rests on table-level access controls, column masking, and audit logs that record who queried or exported data. Model training and inference inside the platform reduce the risk of copying sensitive rows to unmanaged storage, but they do not remove the need for lineage from source table to model output. Provenance is maintained through catalog entries, schema versions, and model cards that link a deployed model to the SQL tables and feature definitions it was built from. Rights questions include who may use a table for training, whether a model output inherits access restrictions from its inputs, and how long derived data may be retained.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Warehouse and lakehouse platforms are converging on a single governed copy of data that serves both SQL analytics and model inference. Open table formats and catalogs are making it easier to move workloads between engines without losing access controls or lineage. The growth of Model Context Protocol servers, including the 262 for SQL databases and warehouses tracked by this site, points toward AI assistants that query governed tables directly rather than through exported files. Over time, more model training and fine-tuning is likely to happen inside or adjacent to the warehouse, with the SQL engine acting as the control point for data access.
